claims.text: Conventionally processed W–Cu composites have a heterogeneous interphase and only moderate continuity of the Cu phase.
The proposed intervention is a single optimized HIP cycle at approximately 950–1050 °C under high pressure for a controlled duration.
HIP promotes interfacial diffusion and wetting between tungsten and copper.
HIP improves bonding at W/Cu interfaces.
Enhanced diffusion during HIP reduces voids and defects at W/Cu interfaces.
Improved interfacial bonding produces a more uniform and continuous copper network within the tungsten matrix.
Greater Cu-phase connectivity reduces interfacial thermal resistance.
Reduced thermal resistance and interfacial defects enable more efficient electron and phonon transport through the copper phase.
The optimized HIP treatment will increase overall thermal conductivity relative to an otherwise comparable conventionally processed W–Cu composite.
The HIP-treated composite will retain the mechanical durability of the untreated baseline.
The HIP-treated composite will retain the irradiation resistance of the untreated baseline.
The refractory tungsten constituent maintains the composite's mechanical strength after HIP.
The refractory tungsten constituent provides irradiation stability.
The beneficial effect requires HIP conditions that do not cause excessive tungsten grain growth.
The beneficial effect requires HIP conditions that do not produce unwanted interfacial phases.
Extreme HIP conditions may compromise mechanical integrity or irradiation resistance.
Controlled cooling after HIP can preserve mechanical and irradiation-resistant properties under heat-dissipation and fusion-joint operating conditions.
The magnitude of the conductivity enhancement is sensitive to HIP temperature, pressure, and duration.
Long-term post-HIP irradiation behavior remains unverified.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant conductivity increase, or measurable degradation of mechanical durability or irradiation resistance, would falsify the hypothesis.
